title: Rethinking Dead Block Prediction for Intermittent Computing
problem: Existing dead block predictors, designed for conventional always-on systems, are ineffective in energy-harvesting intermittent computing systems because they do not account for power failures that invalidate cache blocks before they can be reused, causing unnecessary leakage energy waste on blocks that are nominally 'live' but will be lost.
method: EDBP (Enhanced Dead Block Predictor) augments existing dead block predictors with a power-failure-aware prediction layer. It identifies cache blocks that, though predicted live by a conventional predictor, are unlikely to be accessed before the next anticipated power failure. These blocks are deactivated (gated off) to eliminate leakage energy, freeing energy budget for forward execution. EDBP is combined with the Cache Decay predictor to achieve near-theoretical-minimum cache leakage across 20 Mediabench and MiBench applications.

title: Neoscope: How Resilient Is My SoC to Workload Churn?
problem: Hardware lifetimes are increasing while software workloads evolve rapidly, so SoCs optimized for today's workloads may perform poorly against future workloads; architects lack quantitative tools to design for long-term performance resilience.
method: Neoscope introduces two workload-change metrics, Magnitude and Disruption, that quantitatively characterize how a workload evolves over time, classifying churn as Minimal, Perturbing, Escalating, or Volatile. Using these metrics, Neoscope formulates SoC design space exploration as an integer linear program (ILP) combined with job-shop scheduling concepts, enabling it to find near-globally-optimal SoC configurations for a given churn span in a single invocation rather than requiring exhaustive parameter sweeps. The framework is multi-objective and can optimize simultaneously for performance, area, energy, cost, and carbon efficiency.

title: I-DGNN: A Graph Dissimilarity-based Framework for Designing Scalable and Efficient DGNN Accelerators
problem: Dynamic Graph Neural Network (DGNN) execution requires passing each graph snapshot through the entire DGNN pipeline from layer to layer, generating excessive intermediate data and off-chip memory access, even when consecutive snapshots differ only slightly.
method: I-DGNN proposes a one-pass DGNN computing model that extracts graph update as a chained matrix multiplication between evolving graphs through rigorous mathematical derivation, decoupling inter-snapshot computation from the full DGNN pipeline and expressing it as an independent kernel. A unified accelerator architecture is dynamically configured to support the computation characteristics of this model, providing improved data and pipeline parallelism. A new dataflow and mapping tailored to I-DGNN improves data locality for inter-kernel data across the DGNN pipeline. The framework reduces intermediate data movement across layers.

title: PCcheck: Persistent Concurrent Checkpointing for ML
problem: Checkpointing large ML training runs to persistent storage introduces high overhead when done at high frequency, yet infrequent checkpointing leads to long recovery times after failures — a growing problem as training scale increases and cheap spot VMs dramatically raise failure rates.
method: PCcheck introduces persistent concurrent checkpointing, where model parameter checkpoints are taken concurrently with ongoing training (overlapping checkpoint I/O with compute) while also ensuring persistence to durable storage. It uses a combination of copy-on-write snapshots of model state and pipelined multi-stage I/O to overlap CPU-to-storage transfers with GPU computation. The system tracks consistency across concurrent training steps to guarantee that the checkpoint captured is valid and recoverable, minimizing pause time during the checkpoint process.

title: ARTEMIS: Agile Discovery of Efficient Real-Time Systems-on-Chips in the Heterogeneous Era
problem: Design space exploration (DSE) for heterogeneous real-time SoCs (targeting applications like autonomous driving and AR/VR) must jointly optimize microarchitectural parameters and dynamic task-to-hardware mappings under deadline, power, and area constraints, resulting in an intractably large combined design space.
method: ARTEMIS integrates a dynamic SoC-level scheduler into the DSE loop to eliminate the mapping dimension from the search space, dramatically pruning the effective design space. The scheduler incorporates policies such as task procrastination and memory-traffic/energy-aware task assignment. DSE heuristics use real-time deadline-aware and power/area-aware ranking mechanisms to guide the remaining architecture search. The method is validated on FPGA hardware and evaluated on autonomous vehicle and AR/VR application suites.

title: Optimizing Quantum Circuits, Fast and Slow
problem: Quantum circuit optimization requires balancing two complementary approaches: fast rewrite-rule passes (local pattern matching, low quality) and slow unitary synthesis (global search over circuit space, high quality but exponential cost), but these have been treated as disjoint techniques without a unified framework that exploits their synergies. No prior optimizer systematically combines the two in a way that achieves better quality than either alone.
method: The paper presents a unifying framework that models rewriting and resynthesis as abstract circuit transformation operators on subcircuits. The algorithm 'guoq' alternates between fast rewrite-rule passes (which simplify local patterns and create resynthesis opportunities) and targeted unitary synthesis (applied to subcircuits identified as high-gain by the rewriting pass). Resynthesis is applied to subcircuits of bounded size where exhaustive search is tractable, guided by the rewriting pass which determines which regions are best candidates. This fast-slow interleaving lets rewriting decompose the circuit into manageable blocks for synthesis, while synthesis achieves global optima that local rules cannot reach.

title: HALO: Loop-aware Bootstrapping Management for Fully Homomorphic Encryption
problem: FHE programs using repeated multiplications deplete the ciphertext noise budget (level), requiring bootstrapping to reset it; existing compiler-based bootstrapping placement tools cannot handle loops, severely limiting automated support for practical FHE programs that use iterative constructs.
method: HALO is a compiler that extends automatic bootstrapping placement to programs containing loops. It performs loop-aware level analysis to track ciphertext noise levels across loop iterations, determines the minimum set of bootstrapping operations required to prevent level underflow throughout the loop body and across all iterations, and inserts them automatically. The compiler reasons about loop-carried level dependencies to place bootstrapping at loop boundaries or within the loop body only where necessary.

title: Medusa: Accelerating Serverless LLM Inference with Materialization
problem: Serverless LLM inference suffers from excessive cold-start latency caused by three distinct loading stages: model weight loading to device memory, KV cache initialization (profiling and reserving memory), and CUDA graph capturing for different batch sizes—all of which must repeat on every cold start and negate serverless scalability benefits.
method: Medusa uses materialization: it pre-computes and persists the KV cache initialization state and the CUDA graphs for all relevant batch sizes as serialized artifacts on fast storage (materialized snapshots), so that cold starts bypass both stages entirely and load the pre-built state directly to the GPU. The system manages a catalog of materialized snapshots per model and batching configuration, and restores them during cold start with minimal deserialization overhead. The materialization is done offline or lazily on first warm start.

title: Phi: Leveraging Pattern-based Hierarchical Sparsity for High-Efficiency Spiking Neural Networks
problem: Spiking Neural Network (SNN) accelerators exploit binary activation sparsity (0-1 spikes) to skip zero computations, but they ignore the structured distribution patterns present in spike activations, leaving significant compute savings unexploited. Existing designs treat each non-zero spike independently, incurring redundant runtime multiply-accumulate operations.
method: Phi introduces a two-level hierarchical sparsity framework for SNNs. Level 1 is vector-wise sparsity: spike activations are represented using a small set of pre-defined patterns selected offline via k-means clustering, enabling offline pre-computation of pattern-weight products so that most runtime multiply-accumulates are eliminated. Level 2 is element-wise sparsity: a highly sparse residual matrix (the complement of the Level 1 approximation) handles remaining activations, further reducing computation while preserving accuracy. A pattern-aware fine-tuning technique is applied to increase Level 2 sparsity. The Phi hardware architecture processes both levels on-the-fly, with dedicated datapaths for each sparsity tier.

title: SPARK: Sparsity Aware, Low Area, Energy-Efficient, Near-memory Architecture for Accelerating Linear Programming Problems
problem: Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and Linear Programming (LP) solvers run for tens of hours on large parallel computers because their sparse, branch-intensive algorithms are poorly matched to CPUs and GPUs. GPUs suffer from thread divergence on ILP branching and require frequent host interactions, while CPU solvers like Gurobi cannot meet real-time decision thresholds (seconds to minutes).
method: SPARK reconfigures the existing L1 cache in a CPU to act as a near-cache compute accelerator with ~1.4% area overhead. It integrates sparsity detection and sparsity-aware compute units near the cache to skip insignificant multiplications in sparse matrix operations, and exploits reuse patterns inherent to ILP algorithms (e.g., simplex pivots, branch-and-bound traversal) through a reuse-aware datapath. The architecture is reconfigurable to handle both sparse and dense ILPs and LPs without separate hardware.

title: TNIC: A Trusted NIC Architecture: A hardware-network substrate for building high-performance trustworthy distributed systems
problem: Distributed systems deployed in heterogeneous cloud environments face Byzantine failures from untrusted hardware and software, but existing trusted execution environments (TEEs) are CPU-centric and incur high performance overhead when attempting to enforce network-level trust guarantees such as non-equivocation and transferable authentication.
method: TNIC builds a minimal, formally verified silicon root-of-trust at the NIC level using SmartNIC hardware. It provides two core cryptographic primitives—transferable authentication (signed message delivery) and non-equivocation (monotonic counters preventing double-send attacks)—implemented in hardware-accelerated network processing logic. The TCB is minimized by placing trust enforcement at the network interface, making it CPU-agnostic. TNIC exposes programming APIs and a recipe for constructing Byzantine-fault-tolerant distributed protocols, demonstrated via four trustworthy distributed systems built on the substrate.

title: Snowplow: Effective Kernel Fuzzing with a Learned White-box Test Mutator
problem: Kernel fuzzers rely on program mutation to generate test programs that explore new kernel code paths, but existing mutation heuristics are unable to navigate the complex control and data flow of kernel code to produce mutations that trigger target code locations or increase coverage, resulting in low fuzzing effectiveness.
method: Snowplow uses a learned white-box test mutator that employs machine learning to guide mutation decisions based on kernel code analysis (control flow graphs and data flow) rather than purely random or hand-coded heuristics. The model is trained to predict which system call insertions, argument value changes, or structural mutations are most likely to move execution toward uncovered or target code regions. The white-box analysis of kernel source provides the coverage feedback signal used during training and inference.

title: TempGraph: An Efficient Chain-driven Temporal Graph Computing Framework on the GPU
problem: Temporal graph path problems require vertices to be processed sequentially along time-dependent chains, creating inherently poor parallelism and slow convergence that prevents existing GPU solutions from utilizing the massive thread-level parallelism and high memory bandwidth of modern GPUs.
method: TempGraph transforms the temporal graph into disjoint time-dependent chains that expose temporal dependencies explicitly, then employs a Generate-Activate-Compute (GAC) execution model to decouple temporal dependencies between different chains by maintaining a set of shortcut references. This allows multiple chains to be processed concurrently by massive GPU thread pools while shortcut maintenance handles cross-chain dependency resolution, enabling fast convergence and high parallelism.

title: Squeezing Operator Performance Potential for the Ascend Architecture
problem: Huawei's Ascend domain-specific architecture requires manual management of memory operations and operator execution, creating complex performance bottlenecks that are difficult to diagnose with existing roofline models. Existing roofline models suffer from visualization complexity and inaccurate performance assessment when applied to Ascend's component-level architecture.
method: The paper introduces a component-based roofline model that abstracts individual hardware components (compute units, memory subsystems, data pipelines) to capture per-component performance ceilings and identify bottleneck components. This model is combined with a structured optimization process derived from practical operator optimization case studies on Ascend, identifying common performance issues (e.g., memory bandwidth saturation, pipeline bubbles) and their targeted optimization strategies.

title: NOVA: A Novel Vertex Management Architecture for Scalable Graph Processing
problem: Existing graph processing hardware accelerators require temporal graph partitioning to fit the working set into on-chip memory, limiting scalability to large graphs and causing bandwidth inefficiency from repeated DRAM accesses across partition sweeps.
method: NOVA decouples reduction and propagation operations in the vertex-centric graph processing paradigm, allowing the entire working set to reside in off-chip DRAM rather than being partitioned across on-chip memory. On-chip memory is repurposed as a prefetch/access buffer to hide DRAM latency rather than as a traditional cache holding graph state. The design enables spatial tiling across multiple NOVA nodes for scale-out, achieving near-perfect weak and strong scaling. A cycle-accurate gem5-based model validates the architecture.

title: Concurrency-Informed Orchestration for Serverless Functions
problem: Serverless FaaS platforms suffer excessive cold starts because existing container keep-alive policies ignore concurrent invocations: they fail to reason about whether reusing a busy container (delayed warm start) or cold-starting a new container is preferable, and they make imbalanced eviction decisions that prematurely evict soon-to-be-reused containers.
method: CIDRE is a container orchestration algorithm that combines fine-grained container-level state (busy/idle, time-to-free) with coarse-grained concurrency signals to speculatively decide between a delayed warm start and a cold start under concurrent scaling. For eviction, CIDRE uses both container-level recency and concurrency-aware reuse probability to produce balanced eviction decisions that avoid removing containers still likely to be reused. The algorithm is evaluated on two production FaaS workload traces.
